faqs.answer: Because area grows with the square of the diameter. A 9-inch pan is 12.5 percent wider than an 8-inch pan, but 1.125 squared is 1.27, so the floor is about 26 percent bigger. Width fools the eye. Area does not.
faqs.question: Why is one inch such a big difference?

faqs.answer: Yes, and the cake will be about a fifth shallower. Check it 5 to 10 minutes early, because a thinner layer sets faster and dries out faster. It works fine for a snack cake. Scale it for a layer cake you plan to split and fill.
faqs.question: Can I bake the 8-inch recipe in the 9-inch pan without scaling?

faqs.answer: Not at the same depth. Scale the batter by 1.26 and the layer sits exactly as deep as it did in the 8-inch pan, so it bakes in the same time at the same temperature.
faqs.question: Does the bake time change?

faqs.answer: Scale the whole batch by 1.26 and split it between two 9-inch rounds, or scale each layer on its own. The maths is the same either way, and each layer still takes the recipe time.
faqs.question: What about a two-layer cake?

parts.meaning: The area of an 8-inch round in square inches: 3.14 x 4 x 4.

formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 1.26. Factor = new area divided by old area = 63.6 divided by 50.3 = 1.26.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: A 9-inch round covers 63.6 square inches and an 8-inch round covers 50.3. Divide 63.6 by 50.3 and the factor is 1.26.

howToSteps.name: Scale every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Multiply each ingredient by 1.26, including the leavening. A recipe with 4 cups of batter becomes 5.1 cups.

howToSteps.name: Check the fill
howToSteps.text: Pour the scaled batter into a greased 9-inch round pan. It should sit between half and two-thirds full, no higher.

howToSteps.name: Bake as the recipe says
howToSteps.text: Same oven temperature, same bake time. Test with a toothpick at the recipe time.

title: 8-Inch Round to 9-Inch Round Pan
tutorial: One inch sounds like nothing on a cake pan, and it is a quarter of the recipe. Area grows with the square of the diameter, so moving from 8 inches to 9 inches multiplies the floor by 1.26, not by 1.12. An 8-inch round covers 50.3 square inches and a 9-inch round covers 63.6. That is the whole surprise of this swap: a small change in width is a big change in batter.

Wilton puts numbers on it from the test kitchen: one 8-inch layer takes 4 cups of batter, and one 9-inch layer takes 5. That matches the area maths, since 4 cups scaled by 1.26 is 5.1 cups. If your 8-inch recipe makes 4 cups, the 9-inch version needs just over 5. A recipe that makes 3 cups needs 3.8.

Pour the 8-inch batter into the 9-inch pan without scaling and the layer bakes about a fifth shallower. A thinner layer sets faster and dries out faster, so check it 5 to 10 minutes early and do not leave it in for the full recipe time out of habit. It will still taste like the same cake. It will just be a shorter one, and a shorter layer is harder to split and fill.

Fill the 9-inch pan no more than two-thirds full, which is about 5.3 cups in a pan that holds 8 cups to the rim. Most scaled 8-inch recipes land under that without trying. The one to watch is a recipe that already fills the 8-inch pan to two-thirds: scaled by 1.26 it fills the 9-inch pan to the same two-thirds, which is exactly where it should be.

Bake at the same temperature and the same time. Both pans are 2 inches deep and the scaled batter sits at the same depth, so the heat reaches the middle on the same schedule. The only thing that changes besides the batter is the frosting: a 9-inch top is about a quarter bigger than an 8-inch top, so make about a quarter more frosting to cover it the same way.
